study.title: Exodus 12 The Passover, the judgment, and the exit of Egypt
study.overview: Exodus 12 describes the Passover institution, the protection granted by the blood of the lamb, the continued obligation of the feast of unleavened bread, and finally the departure of Israel from Egypt after the judgment on the firstborn. The chapter unites redemption and judgment: God frees his people as he executes judgment against Egypt and his gods. The narrative shows that deliverance is not born of the strength of Israel, but from the word of the LORD, from obedience to his commandment and from the sign of blood in the houses.

outline.title: The Institution of Easter
outline.explanation: God redefines Israel's calendar and gives detailed instructions for lamb, blood at the gates, the hasty meal and the annual memory of deliverance. Easter marks the beginning of a new national and liturgical life under the direction of the LORD.

outline.title: The Feast of the Bloops without yeast
outline.explanation: For seven days, the people should remove yeast and eat only yeast-free breads. The celebration included holy assemblies and the seriousness of the removal of any transgression, extending both to the natural and the resident foreigner.

outline.title: The obedience of Moses and the catechesis of memory
outline.explanation: Moses transmits to the elders the orders received, including the application of blood with hyssop and stay inside the house until the morning. The chapter also predicts that the children will ask for the rite, and the answer should link the ceremony to God's saving act in Egypt.

outline.title: The final judgment on Egypt and the departure of Israel
outline.explanation: At midnight the LORD strikes the firstborn of Egypt; Pharaoh then casts out Israel. The people hurriedly take away, taking mass without yeast and receiving favor to ask the Egyptians for goods. The chapter concludes with the length of stay in Egypt, the night of vigil for the LORD and additional rules of the Passover, culminating in the organized exit of Israel as armies under the divine direction.

study.context: The text is still in the land of Egypt, in the context of plagues and increasing pressure on Pharaoh. Tyndale's notes indicate that the month mentioned corresponds to the month Abibe, later called Nisã, and that the feast celebrated a historic event in which God defeated death and freed his people from slavery. The chapter also presupposes a structured community life in families, elders and future generations, with the celebration functioning as a pedagogical memorial of redemption.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter presents God as a sovereign judge and faithful redeemer. The blood of the lamb functions as a sign of protection, showing that the spared life is under the divine provision and not of human merit. The repetition of the liturgical memory teaches that salvation must be remembered and transmitted, untreated as an isolated event. The exclusion of the yeast and the hurry of the meal communicate separation, urgency and readiness to obey. The text also emphasizes the holiness of the people who are called to belong to the Lord in contrast to Egypt, and obedience needs the commandment as part of the proper response to redemption. In evangelical Christian reading, many see here a foreshadowing of the redemptive work of Christ and of the Lord's supper, but this connection must be read as theological interpretation, not as an explicit affirmation of the text of Exodus.

scholarViews.insight: The month of Abibe marks the beginning of Israel's religious calendar, and the feast commemorates a historical fact: God defeated death and rescued his people from Egypt's slavery.
The blood on the shoulder pads and in the verga shows that the safety of Israel depended on the sprinkled blood; the judgment would pass over the houses marked by this sign.
The expression "miroes" indicates that Israel went out in order, as hosts or organized troops, under the direction of God himself.

questions: What does the text teach about the relationship between redemption and obedience: Was Israel saved because of blood and also called to act according to the order received?
Why did the memory of Easter need to be repeated to every generation, and how does it shape the faith of God's people today?
How do the separation of yeast and the hasty exit teach spiritual readiness and break with ancient slavery?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to trust in God's provision for deliverance, to obey precisely what he commands and to cultivate grateful memory. In practice, this can mean: deliberately remember the acts of God in prayer and at home; treat worship as a serious response to salvation; abandon habits that symbolize corruption and spiritual delay; and teach the new generations that deliverance comes from the LORD, not from human strength. The biblical faith here is not passive: it listens, prepares, acts and celebrates.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are brief and do not cover all the details of the chapter. It was not possible to verify the meaning of all symbols other than the text and commentators inform. Connections with Christ and the Lord's supper belong to the later Christian interpretation and should not be read as a direct explanation of the immediate meaning of Exodus 12. No external historical data other than that appears in the notes provided were also included.
